```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  prompt = FALSE
)
source_roots <- c(".", "..")
source_roots <- source_roots[
  file.exists(file.path(source_roots, "DESCRIPTION"))
]
if (length(source_roots) && requireNamespace("pkgload", quietly = TRUE)) {
  pkgload::load_all(
    source_roots[[1L]],
    quiet = TRUE,
    export_all = FALSE
  )
} else {
  library(readPBOC)
}

package_file <- function(...) {
  pieces <- c(...)
  relative <- do.call(file.path, as.list(pieces))
  candidates <- c(
    file.path(source_roots, "inst", relative),
    system.file(..., package = "readPBOC")
  )
  found <- candidates[
    nzchar(candidates) & file.exists(candidates) & !dir.exists(candidates)
  ]
  if (!length(found)) {
    stop("Could not find packaged file ", paste(pieces, collapse = "/"))
  }
  normalizePath(found[[1L]], winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE)
}

money_cells <- utils::read.csv(
  package_file("extdata", "readpboc-worksheet-fixture.csv"),
  header = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = "",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
html_fixture <- package_file("extdata", "readpboc-table-fixture.html")
catalog_snapshot <- readRDS(package_file(
  "examples", "data", "pboc-current-series-catalog.rds"
))
values_snapshot <- readRDS(package_file(
  "examples", "data", "pboc-current-series-values.rds"
))
release_snapshot <- readRDS(package_file(
  "examples", "data", "pboc-release-index.rds"
))
```

`readPBOC` separates discovery from reading. Discovery follows the official
archive and returns metadata; reading consumes a catalog row, URL, or local
path. This separation is useful when you want to inspect coverage before
downloading anything, or when an audit requires the exact source URL beside
the observations.

## Understand coverage before reading

There is no single package-wide series start date. Discovery reflects the
current PBOC indexes, and a year row only says that the parser recognised a
year-labelled link. Chinese and English pages are separate inventories rather
than paired translations. At the live check used for this documentation on 25
August 2026, recognised Chinese year rows ran from 1999 through 2026 and
English year-labelled rows from 2001 through 2026. The 2026 section check
returned six Chinese sections and no English section rows, illustrating why a
year link alone is not evidence that a particular English workbook is
available.

The installed offline snapshots record a fixed, auditable subset:

```{r packaged-coverage}
series_key <- paste(
  values_snapshot$revision_id,
  values_snapshot$sheet,
  values_snapshot$table,
  values_snapshot$series,
  sep = " / "
)

coverage_summary <- data.frame(
  evidence = c("Numeric workbooks", "Numeric observations", "Table/series combinations", "Distinct series labels", "Release-index rows"),
  count = c(
    nrow(catalog_snapshot),
    nrow(values_snapshot),
    length(unique(series_key)),
    length(unique(values_snapshot$series)),
    nrow(release_snapshot)
  )
)
knitr::kable(coverage_summary, row.names = FALSE)
```

The 26 numeric workbooks are all sourced from the Chinese 2026 archive. Their
coverage by subject is:

```{r packaged-subjects}
subject_counts <- sort(table(catalog_snapshot$section_id), decreasing = TRUE)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    section_id = names(subject_counts),
    workbooks = as.integer(subject_counts)
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

These groups cover aggregate-financing flow and stock; CGPI; credit-fund
sources and uses for several institution/currency groupings; Shibor, bond
yields, interbank lending and repos, debt securities, and stock markets; and
money supply, exchange rates, reserves, overseas-held RMB assets, and monetary
and depository-sector balance sheets.

The workbook titles below are the complete numeric snapshot inventory. The
count is the number of distinct `series` labels in each workbook, not a promise
that every label has the same periods.

```{r packaged-workbooks}
workbook_inventory <- aggregate(
  series ~ section_id + release_title_en,
  values_snapshot,
  function(x) length(unique(x))
)
names(workbook_inventory)[3] <- "series_labels"
workbook_inventory <- workbook_inventory[
  order(workbook_inventory$section_id, workbook_inventory$release_title_en),
]
knitr::kable(workbook_inventory, row.names = FALSE)
```

For the exact label-level inventory, keep the revision and workbook title with
the label because names can recur across workbooks:

```{r exact-series-inventory}
series_inventory <- unique(values_snapshot[c(
  "revision_id", "section_id", "release_title_en", "series"
)])
series_inventory <- series_inventory[order(
  series_inventory$section_id,
  series_inventory$release_title_en,
  series_inventory$series
), ]

# Show the first entries; print series_inventory for the complete inventory.
utils::head(series_inventory, 12)
```

Most monthly tables contain January–June 2026. Financial-market workbooks end
in May, Domestic RMB Financial Assets Held by Overseas Entities ends in March,
and the reserves/liquidity template contains one 30 June point-in-time column.
Every stored row has a non-missing `period` and numeric `value`, but the panel
is not balanced. In Statistics of Interbank Pledged Repo, six-month trading
volume has no April row; nine-month and one-year trading volume have no January
or May row. An absent observation is missing or unreported, never an implied
zero.

Gap checks should be scoped to one revision and series because labels can
repeat across workbooks. This deterministic check confirms that the two Money
Supply series used in Getting Started each contain all six expected months:

```{r check-monthly-gaps}
money <- values_snapshot[
  values_snapshot$revision_id == "2026071516481518348" &
    values_snapshot$series %in% c("Money", "Money & Quasi-money"),
  c("series", "period", "value"),
  drop = FALSE
]

monthly_coverage <- function(period) {
  dates <- sort(unique(as.Date(
    paste0(sub("\\.", "-", period), "-01")
  )))
  expected <- seq.Date(min(dates), max(dates), by = "month")
  missing <- setdiff(expected, dates)
  data.frame(
    first = min(dates),
    last = max(dates),
    observations = length(dates),
    missing_months = if (length(missing)) {
      paste(format(missing, "%Y-%m"), collapse = ", ")
    } else {
      "none"
    }
  )
}

money_coverage <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(split(money$period, money$series), monthly_coverage)
)
knitr::kable(money_coverage)
```

Language is source provenance, not label language. All 3,095 numeric rows have
`language == "zh"` and a non-missing `series_en`; 2,605 also have
`series_zh`, while 490 carry an English-only series label. The release snapshot
is different: it contains 740 Chinese index rows dated 17 April 2001–15 July
2026 and 692 English rows dated 11 July 2002–15 July 2026. Those rows use
different feed categories and are not guaranteed translations of each other.

## Discover the archive (online)

The discovery functions read the official PBOC indexes over HTTPS. They return
tibbles and do not write a cache. The Chinese and English indexes are queried
independently: the Chinese archive is commonly more current, while the English
archive can have narrower coverage and different section titles.

The following is a small live workflow for an interactive session. The guard
means it is not run by CRAN or by an offline vignette build.

```{r live-discovery, eval=TRUE}
if (interactive()) {
  years <- pboc_years("both")
  sections <- pboc_sections(2026, "both")
  catalog <- pboc_catalog(
    2026,
    language = "both",
    section = "money",
    formats = c("xlsx", "xls")
  )

  list(
    years = head(years),
    sections = head(sections),
    catalog = head(catalog)
  )
}
```

`pboc_years()` returns `year` and `language`. `pboc_sections()` adds a
canonical `section_id`, bilingual section labels, and the source URL.
`pboc_catalog()` returns a `pboc_resource_index` tibble with stable
`asset_id`, a publication-specific `revision_id`, year/language/section/item
metadata, format, publication date, attachment URL, and source index URL.
`asset_id` identifies the conceptual attachment across revisions; use
`revision_id` when preserving an exact publication.

## Read the same kind of data offline

The reading layer can execute without the network. The small worksheet and
HTML document are author-created structural fixtures under the package
license; they contain no PBOC product data and are included only to exercise
the readers offline.

First normalise the worksheet cells directly:

```{r tidy-fixture}
money <- pboc_tidy(money_cells)
stopifnot(all(c("series", "period", "value", "value_raw") %in% names(money)))

money[c("series", "series_zh", "series_en", "period", "value")]
```

For a local HTML table, `pboc_read()`
uses `rvest::html_table()`. One table is returned as a data frame/tibble; if
the page contains multiple tables, a list of tables is returned. The packaged
structural HTML fixture is read from its local path and is not downloaded
again:

```{r html-fixture}
html_table <- pboc_read(html_fixture)
stopifnot(is.data.frame(html_table) || is.list(html_table))

html_info <- list(
  class = class(html_table),
  dimensions = if (is.data.frame(html_table)) dim(html_table) else lengths(html_table),
  source_path = basename(attr(html_table, "source_path")),
  source_url = attr(html_table, "source_url")
)
html_info
```

For a local spreadsheet, `sheet = 1` reads the first sheet and `sheet = NA`
reads every non-empty sheet into a named list. `tidy = TRUE` asks
`pboc_read()` to read spreadsheet cells as text and pass them through
`pboc_tidy()`. HTML tables are parsed as supplied by the source markup; they
are not passed through the spreadsheet normaliser.

## Select one table with `pboc_data()`

`pboc_data()`
combines catalog filtering and reading for one matching workbook. Its
`language = "auto"` mode tries the Chinese archive first and falls back to the
English archive when that attempt errors or returns no matching row. It still
requires a sufficiently specific `section` and, when necessary, `item`; an
ambiguous or empty match is an error rather than an arbitrary selection.

Use it interactively when you want the current official data:

```{r live-data, eval=TRUE}
if (interactive()) {
  money_supply <- pboc_data(
    year = 2026,
    section = "money",
    item = "Money Supply",
    language = "auto",
    tidy = TRUE
  )
  head(money_supply)
}
```

The returned object follows the `pboc_read()`
contract: a tibble for one sheet, or a named list when all sheets are read.
For a tidied workbook, expect the long-form columns described in the
`pboc_tidy()`
reference, including `period`, numeric `value`, `value_raw`, and source
coordinates. Source metadata are carried as attributes where available.

## Choose the right preservation layer

* Use `pboc_read()` for analysis when the source is a spreadsheet or HTML
  table.
* Use `pboc_tidy()` when the worksheet has bilingual, multi-row headers or
  period columns and you need a stable long form with audit coordinates.
* Use `pboc_download()`
  when an attachment must be retained exactly, including a PDF. PDF extraction
  is intentionally not normalised by `readPBOC`; downloading preserves the
  official artifact for a separate PDF workflow.

Because the PBOC pages are public but not an API contract, HTML structure and
workbook layout can change. Keep the catalog row and source URL with derived
data, and treat parser warnings or schema changes as review points rather than
silently coercing them.
